target_claim: For every prime p, work in the finite field \(\mathbb F_p\). Define \(\tau:\mathbb F_p\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\) by \(\tau(0)=0\); for \(b\ne0\), let \(\tau(b)\) be the smallest nonnegative integer \(r\) such that \(2^r\in\{-b,b\}\), and set \(\tau(b)=\infty\) if no such \(r\) exists. Let \(\Omega=\{b\in\mathbb F_p:\tau(b)<\infty\}\). Define the matrix \(P\), indexed by \(\Omega\times\Omega\), by \(P(x,0)=P(x,2x)=1/2\) for every \(x\in\Omega\setminus\{0\}\), \(P(0,1)=P(0,-1)=1/2\), and \(P(x,y)=0\) otherwise. Then \(P\) is aperiodic: for every \(x\in\Omega\), \(\gcd\{t\in\mathbb N^+:P^t(x,x)>0\}=1\), where \(P^t\) is the ordinary t-th matrix power. No input-size convention is required because this is a finite mathematical claim, not an asymptotic or algorithmic one.

Let $X_0,X_1,\dots$ be a regular Markov chain on a finite state space $\Omega$ with transfer matrix $P$. That is, for $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and $x,y\in \Omega$, we have $$\mathbb{P}(X_{t+1}=y|X_{t}=x)=P(x,y).$$
From this, if $\mu:\Omega\rightarrow [0,1]$ is the distribution of $X_0$, then $\mu P^{t}$ is the distribution of $X_t$. Say that $P$ is \emph{irreducible} if for every $x,y\in\Omega$ there exists $t\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $P^{t}(x,y)>0$. Also, say that $P$ is \emph{aperiodic} if for every $x\in \Omega$, the greatest common divisor of the elements of the set $\{t\in\mathbb{N}^{+}:P^{t}(x,x)>0\}$ is $1$. We use the following lemma about the convergence of distributions in a Markov chain.

First, let us define our set $H\subset \mathbb{F}_p^{N}$. To this end, let us introduce some further notation. Let $\tau:\mathbb{F}_p\rightarrow \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ be the function defined as follows: $\tau(0)=0$, and if $b\neq 0$, then $\tau(b)$ is the smallest nonnegative integer $r$ such that $2^{r}\in\{-b,b\}$; if there exists no such $r$, then set $\tau(b)=\infty$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{F}_p$ be the set of elements $b$ such that $\tau(b)<\infty$.

			\item $P(0,1)=P(0,-1)=1/2$,
			\item $P(x,y)=0$ otherwise.
		\end{itemize}
